newsitem.title: GREECE: TRUCKERS' ODYSSEY CONTINUES IN GREECE AFTER FRANCE.
newsitem.headline: TRUCKERS' ODYSSEY CONTINUES IN GREECE AFTER FRANCE.

text.p: British lorry driver Alan Kendall sips a beer staring at the forest ahead with a hopeless look. For the past eight days he has been stranded in the middle of nowhere with a cargo of meat in danger of spoiling.

"This is the first time in 35 years that I won't be home for Christmas. I was held up in France by a truckers' strike and now here by the farmers. I want a hot shower and a good meal but above all I want to move on," he said.

Kendall's truck, with 20 tonnes of frozen meat destined for Azerbaijan, is among hundreds of stranded lorries in this central Greek forest area by a farmers' barricade a few hundred metres to the north.

The drivers come from England, Turkey, Bulgaria, Germany, Iran, Italy and Denmark. They prepare dinner, mostly chicken and rice, on camp-stoves but a sudden downpour sends them running back in their cabs.

"We are people not animals," said Kendall, who hasn't shaved in four days. "We have been using the forest for a toilet. The farmers brought us some pork chops and chips for the first time after seven days."
"But the gesture didn't make colleagues from Iran and Turkey happy because they are Moslems and don't eat pork. They told them that's it. Take it or leave it," he added.

When the eight-thirty news comes on, the drivers anxiously gather in front of a battery-powered television set in hope of an announcement that the farmers' nationwide blockade, now in its 12th day, is over.
"Please tell me what this guy is saying," says Bulgarian driver Pimcho Atanasov pointing at farmers' representative Yannis Pattakis, the most frequent face on television since the blockade began.
"I am out of diesel trying to keep warm and keeping my cargo of margarine from going bad. Now it's spoiled ... I don't care anymore ... I just want to go back home to Sofia," he said.
He pulls out of his pocket 3,000 drachmas ($15). "This is all I have left. I don't know what's going to happen if I stay here another day."

But Pattakis has no good news. "We will continue our struggle until the government gives in to our just demands. We understand the problems we have caused but the government holds the key to freeing up the roads."
A thick fog gradually covers the area. The drivers go silent and slowly drag their feet back to their trucks for another cold night with some cheap brandy to keep them warm.
The mood at the farmers' barricades is different. In Tempi, farmers roast a lamb on a spit, sitting on plastic chairs around a bonfire which gleams through the fog.

They play cards under a makeshift tent with a local band playing bouzouki songs. The smell of smoked meat mixes up with that of burning rubber from the tyres in the bonfire and the farmers drink shots of ouzo and make jokes about the government.
"We don't have to go back in the fields until March. If the government doesn't give us cheaper fuel and better prices it better have a lot of patience," cotton grower Aris Manolopoulos said.
The farmers have set up some 90 barricades on the national road network with 10,000 tractors blocking traffic in an area of 1,500 kms.

The main north-south highway linking Athens and the northern port-city of Salonika alternates scenes of blockading tractors and queues of stranded lorries -- with police in the middle to avert clashes. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
